title: Time-resolved study of carbonization and growth of ultrathin 3C-SiC on Si(111) under ultra-high vacuum
authors: Pranjali Jadhao, Mojdeh Fallahpour, Josef Polčák, Eva Kolíbalová, Michal Horák, Jan Michalička, Petr Bábor, Stanislav Voborný, Tomáš Šikola
abstract: The early-stage formation of silicon carbide (SiC) on Si(111) by ethylene exposure under ultra-high vacuum (UHV) was investigated to resolve the time-dependent chemical and morphological evolution of an ultrathin layer. Clean Si(111) substrates were exposed to C$_2$H$_4$ at 800 °C for 2 min to 4 h, and the surfaces followed by in-situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and ex-situ AFM, SEM, AES, SIMS and TEM. Si 2p and C 1s peak analysis shows the progressive conversion of elemental silicon into a carbidic Si-C phase, the SiC fraction overtaking the elemental component between 120 and 160 min and saturating near 80-81% beyond 180 min, leaving about 19-20% residual elemental silicon. Correlative SEM and AFM reveal a parallel morphological progression, from sparse isolated islands to a coalesced, near-continuous layer. AES depth profiling confirms carbon incorporated into the near-surface region rather than weakly adsorbed as contamination, assigning the islands to early SiC nuclei. TEM confirms the zinc-blende lattice and the presence of cubic silicon carbide (3C-SiC). Together, these results provide a time-resolved picture of SiC nucleation, coalescence and layer growth on Si(111), relevant to 3C-SiC heteroepitaxy, and can be utilized in the optimization of SiC/Si(111) templates for growth of III-nitride and other carbide systems on silicon (e.g. Mo$_2$C).
summary: This work provides a comprehensive, time-resolved characterization of how ultrathin 3C-SiC nucleates and grows on Si(111) using ethylene gas at high temperatures. By combining multiple advanced surface analysis techniques (XPS, AFM, STEM), the authors map the chemical conversion from elemental silicon to carbide and track the physical transition from isolated islands to a continuous film. This detailed understanding is crucial for engineering high-quality semiconductor interfaces.
main_problem: To resolve the time-dependent chemical and morphological evolution of an ultrathin silicon carbide (SiC) layer formed on Si(111) during early-stage carbonization.
main_result: The growth proceeds via island nucleation followed by coalescence, resulting in a crystalline 3C-SiC film whose formation is tracked chemically (XPS) and structurally (AFM/STEM).
method: A combination of *in-situ* XPS for chemical tracking, *ex-situ* AFM/SEM for morphology, AES/SIMS for depth profiling, and STEM-EELS for atomic structure confirmation was employed.
model_or_system: The physical system is the heteroepitaxial growth of SiC on a Si(111) substrate using ethylene exposure at 800 °C under UHV conditions.
key_observables: Si/C chemical ratios (XPS, AES), surface roughness evolution (AFM), film thickness ($\sim 9$ nm via STEM-EELS), and crystal structure confirmation ($3	ext{C-SiC}$ polytype).
important_parameters: Growth temperature of $800^\circ	ext{C}$; precursor $	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_4$; time evolution from minutes to hours.
main_assumptions: The growth mechanism is assumed to be governed by surface chemical reactions and island-mediated coalescence, leading to a specific residual elemental Si fraction.
figures_summary: Figures show XPS spectra tracking phase conversion over time; SEM/AFM track the transition from isolated islands to continuous films; STEM-EELS confirm the crystalline structure and interface quality.
paper_structure: The paper follows a progression of characterization techniques: initial chemical monitoring (XPS) establishes the time dependence, followed by morphological mapping (SEM/AFM), detailed elemental profiling (AES/SIMS), and finally atomic structural confirmation (STEM-EELS).
why_interesting: While primarily materials science, the study involves non-equilibrium surface chemistry and phase transitions under controlled vacuum conditions, which touches upon concepts relevant to open quantum systems or reaction dynamics modeling.
